title: Deployable sensor payload
eyebrow: Case study / Union College Rocket Team
description: CHARGER won the Deployable Sensor Payload event at Battle of the Rockets 2026, with custom payload electronics and five live telemetry channels.
lede: A rocket that drops a sensor payload at apogee and streams five channels of telemetry to a handheld ground station. We built CHARGER and it won.
brief_note: There was no rocket team at Union College when I started. I founded it.
Published by Union College and by the competition organizer.

sections.label: The event
paras: A G motor flies the rocket to 700-1,200 feet. On the way down the payload releases the nose cone at 75 percent of peak altitude, and the nose cone has to land under 15 feet per second on its own.
With the nose cone gone, a camera on the payload films the ground until it lands.

sections.label: The airframe
paras: inches across, four trapezoidal balsa fins on a cardboard body tube. Center of gravity at 22 inches, stability margin 1.80 calibers.
Cardboard because the payload transmits from the pad on, and carbon fiber would put a conductive shell around the 2.4 GHz antenna.

sections.label: The numbers
paras: Aerotech G77R-7, thrust to weight 8.17. Simulated apogee 1,033 feet. Descent 13.8 feet per second under a 48 inch ripstop nylon canopy.
list: Four trapezoidal fins, root chord 2.76 in, height 2.36 in, sweep 2.17 in
Stability margin 1.80 cal, centre of gravity at 22 in
Aerotech G77R-7, thrust to weight 8.17, burn 1.25 s
Simulated apogee 1,033 ft, descent 13.8 ft/s on a 48 in parachute
Rail buttons at 2 in from the aft end and 22 in from the nose, near the CG
Rocket $465.42, payload $250.53, ground station $0.00 from existing kit

sections.label: What the rules forced
paras: The event bans commercial flight computers in the payload, so every ejection charge fires off our own board and barometric sensor. The commercial altimeter is only there so a judge can read peak altitude after recovery.
